title: ReelShort as a New Template of International Short-drama Business: Platformisation, Glocalisation, and De-Westernised Practices
finding: Qualitative (content analysis + 12 semi-structured interviews): per authors, ReelShort's success rests on vertically integrated IP and glocalised content, i.e. localised narratives for its primary U.S. market, exporting a media template rather than single episodes; the format is described as fast-paced, quirky, addictive romance on vertical screens.
why_for_us: The exportable thing is the template (pace, vertical framing, serial hooks) filled with local material - so we keep the duanju skeleton but fill it with Polish notary-office specifics rather than imported CEO-romance tropes.

title: The Conversion game: Production mechanisms and power relations in the Chinese micro-drama industry
venue: Convergence The International Journal of Research into New Media Technologies
finding: Qualitative (production ethnography + in-depth interviews): per authors, micro-drama production is a closed loop centred on conversion rate - data-driven recombination of motifs, 'gratification points' and paywalled cliffhangers engineered for emotional conversion, horse-racing mass production, and an outcome decided by distribution ('distribution is king'). No effect sizes reported in the abstract.
why_for_us: Design every episode backwards from one conversion event (for us: click to the product page / next episode) with a gratification beat and an end cliffhanger, and budget as much effort for distribution as for production.

title: New directions in vertical storytelling: creative shifts in micro-drama for mobile audiences
finding: Critically informed review (no new data): per author, mobile-specific conditions - vertical framing, compressed duration, cliff-hanger-led rhythm, rapid genre recycling, audience feedback and AI-assisted production - are reshaping storytelling; the form remains shaped by formulaic repetition, platform analytics, production speed and data-driven risk management.
why_for_us: Confirms the craft checklist for a 60-90 s vertical episode (vertical cinematic language, cliffhanger rhythm, feedback-responsive authorship, AI pipeline) and warns that formula fatigue is the known failure mode.

title: The Impact of Micro-Drama Viewing Motivation on Flow Experience and Continuous Viewing Intention: Evidence from Chinese Users Based on the UTAUT2 Model
venue: Asia-pacific Journal of Convergent Research Interchange
finding: Survey + SEM (10 interviews, then N=774 Chinese viewers; self-report, cross-sectional): per authors, viewing motivation predicted flow (beta=0.628) and continuance intention (beta=0.460); flow raised continuance (beta=0.356) and partially mediated the link (indirect beta=0.296, 95% CI 0.197-0.411).
why_for_us: Continued viewing runs through an uninterrupted 'flow' state, so avoid anything that breaks immersion mid-episode (hard-sell inserts, logo cards) and keep the product moment inside the scene. Weak venue, intention not behaviour.

title: Comparative Study on the Narrative Pace of Online Micro-Short Dramas and Traditional Web Dramas
finding: Case comparison of two titles (A Wonderful New Year vs Hidden Love; qualitative, n=2 works): per authors, narrative turning points arrive significantly earlier in micro-short dramas than in web dramas, with higher climax density and accelerated plot progression, supported by temporal compression, editing rhythm and colour tone.
why_for_us: Put the first turn within the opening seconds and plan several reversals per 60-90 s episode instead of one act break; evidence is a two-title case study only.

title: The Mechanism of "Pleasure Production" under Platform Logic: A Study on the Narrative Structure of Vertical Micro-Dramas A Case Study of I Became a Stepmother in the 1980s
finding: Single-title textual analysis (qualitative): per author, vertical micro-dramas build high-density emotional stimulation through plot compression, frequent conflicts and continuous reversals ('pleasure-oriented' / shuang narrative); recommendation algorithms, retention metrics and monetisation reinforce the pattern and standardise content.
why_for_us: Names the three levers we can borrow at small scale - compression, frequent conflict, continuous reversal - e.g. a client/deadline conflict resolved by the assistant as the episode's gratification beat. Weak venue, one case.

title: Research on the Motivations and Cognitive Changes of Older Groups Watching Micro-Short Dramas in the Smart Media Era
finding: Qualitative (grounded theory, in-depth interviews, N=24 older viewers): per author, five core motivations - social, utilitarian, reciprocal, self-display and altruistic - with viewing moving from individual emotional satisfaction to collective meaning-making.
why_for_us: Micro-drama viewing is not only a youth habit and has social/utilitarian motives; for 40+ notaries and staff, give episodes a practical takeaway and something worth showing a colleague.

title: Narrative adaptation of Chinese short dramas in the European and American markets: exploration of commensurable resources and transcoding strategies
finding: Comparative textual analysis (qualitative): per authors, overseas short dramas rely on emotional commonality and cultural transcoding, and differ from domestic Chinese ones in geographic/cultural attributes, ethical orientation (normative vs virtue ethics), structural integrity, temporal coherence and character portrayal.
why_for_us: Tropes do not travel unchanged: emotions are portable, settings and moral codes are not - so adapt hooks to Polish professional norms (duty, liability, formality) rather than copying revenge/CEO plots.

title: Ethical media creation and consumption in the age of digital fast food: The case of Chinese micro-drama
finding: Conceptual/ethical analysis (no data): the author applies virtue ethics (Aristotle, Confucius, neo-Aristotelian media ethics) to the creation and consumption of micro-dramas, framed as 'digital fast food'.
why_for_us: A sceptical professional audience may read manipulative hooks as cheap; this is the critique to pre-empt by keeping hooks honest and the tone respectful of the profession.

title: How video production affects student engagement: an empirical study of MOOC videos
finding: Platform data (6.9 million video-watching sessions, four edX courses): engagement measured as how long students watch each video and whether they attempt the post-video problem. The OpenAlex abstract states the design but not the specific length/production thresholds, so no numbers are quoted here.
why_for_us: The canonical large-N evidence that production decisions move watch time; use it as method (measure watch-through and the next action per episode), and read the full paper before citing its length guidance.

title: Emotion-Induced Engagement in Internet Video Advertisements
finding: Controlled experiment (facial-expression coding of joy/surprise, eye tracking, zapping as retention): per authors, surprise and joy concentrate attention and retain viewers; the level of surprise matters most for attention, the velocity (rate of change) of joy matters most for retention, and joy gains outweigh joy losses.
why_for_us: Open with a surprise at high level, then build amusement in rising steps rather than one flat joke - retention follows the upward slope of joy, so pace gags as an escalation across the 60-90 s.

title: Understanding Why Consumers Don't Skip Pre-Roll Video Ads
finding: Large industry data set of pre-roll ads (multiple countries and categories; observational): per authors, less complex affective ad characteristics increase skipping, and attention-getting tactics backfire because they make viewers recognise the content as advertising and skip.
why_for_us: In paid placements the first seconds must look like story, not like an ad: no logo sting or shouted claim up front, and enough narrative complexity to occupy the viewer.

title: Brand recall of skippable vs non-skippable ads in YouTube: Readapting information and arousal to active audiences
finding: 3x2 experiment (ad design x skippable/non-skippable, after neuroscientific pre-test): per authors, viewers of skippable ads mainly process information in the initial part of the ad, while for non-skippable ads the high-arousal stimulus should precede the key information to be remembered.
why_for_us: On skippable/swipeable surfaces (Reels, Shorts, feed) the series name and the product cue must appear in the opening seconds; in email or embedded players you can lead with the gag and name the product after it.

title: This Way Up: The Effectiveness of Mobile Vertical Video Marketing
finding: One large-scale field study plus two experiments: per authors, vertical mobile video ads raise consumer interest and engagement versus horizontal ones and are processed more fluently because full-screen viewing needs no phone rotation; the fluency advantage is stronger for Generation Z than for Generations X and Y.
why_for_us: Vertical is the right master format for phone feeds, but the benefit is weaker for our older audience - so also cut a 1:1 or 16:9 version for LinkedIn desktop and email.

title: Exploring user engagement behavior with short-form video advertising on short-form video platforms: a visual-audio perspective
finding: TikTok field data (2,511 product-promotion videos from 60 sellers, regression on computer-vision and speech features): per authors, number of shots and image complexity have inverted-U relations with engagement; vertical format raises comments and shares; faster speech rate raises shares only; higher average spectral centroid lowers likes and comments.
why_for_us: There is an optimum, not a maximum, for cut rate and visual clutter - edit briskly but not frantically, keep frames clean, keep dialogue brisk, and avoid harsh/bright-sounding voice timbre in the AI voices.

title: Analyzing User Engagement with TikTok's Short Format Video Recommendations using Data Donations
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Data donation (347 TikTok users, 9.2M recommended videos): per authors, user attention stays stable at around 45% while daily usage time grows over a user's lifetime, and users like more videos from accounts they follow than from accounts they do not follow.
why_for_us: Assume under half of a recommended video is actually watched, so the product-relevant beat cannot sit only at the end; building followers matters because followed-account videos earn more likes.

title: Unpacking Multimodal Fact-Checking: Features and Engagement of Fact-Checking Videos on Chinese TikTok (Douyin)
finding: Douyin content analysis (4,309 videos, automated + manual coding): per authors, the videos used higher brightness, less cool-colour dominance, faster tempo, clickbait and humour; three types emerged (long storytelling cartoons, short stimulating, short authoritative); several audiovisual features and persuasive strategies were associated with likes, comments and reshares (directions not given in the abstract).
why_for_us: Informational short video for a serious topic still earns engagement through bright, warm, fast, humorous treatment - a usable look-and-feel brief for an office comedy with a factual core.

title: Beyond Views: Measuring and Predicting Engagement in Online Videos
venue: Proceedings of the International AAAI Conference on Web and Social Media
finding: Platform data (5.3 million YouTube videos, 2016): per authors, engagement (watch time, average percentage watched) is stable over time unlike popularity, and is predictable before upload from video context, topic and channel information (R2=0.77); they propose 'relative engagement' calibrated against video properties.
why_for_us: Judge episodes by percentage watched relative to videos of the same length, not by views; views depend on promotion, watch percentage depends on the content and topic we choose.

title: To engage or not engage? The features of video content on YouTube affecting digital consumer engagement
finding: YouTube data (more than 11,000 videos from 150 influencers): per authors, medium-length and long videos posted in non-business hours and on weekdays, with subjective language style, less-active events and temporal indications, get more views, likes and comments; negative or low-arousal emotion also promotes general interest.
why_for_us: Posting outside business hours on weekdays is a testable default for YouTube; note the length finding concerns long-form influencer video and conflicts with short-form evidence (MD040).

title: Investigating the Effectiveness of Product Placements in Television Shows: The Role of Modality and Plot Connection Congruence on Brand Memory and Attitude
finding: Controlled experiment ('theater methodology'): per author, modality (visual/auditory) and plot connection interact - memory improves when modality and plot connection are incongruent, but persuasion is enhanced by congruency; incongruent placements seem out of place, are discounted and hurt brand attitudes.
why_for_us: If a character names the assistant aloud it must matter to the plot; a spoken mention with no story function is remembered but damages attitude. Make the product a plot device, not a line of dialogue.

title: Do you like What you Recognize?
finding: Field experiment with actual moviegoers: per authors, brand recognition is highest for placements that are both highly prominent and strongly plot-connected, whereas brand attitude is most positive when the brand is strongly plot-connected but placed less prominently; recognition mediates the effect of plot connection, not of prominence.
why_for_us: The recognition-attitude trade-off in one study: for a sceptical audience optimise for attitude - strong plot role, modest screen prominence (the assistant solves the problem; no lingering logo shots).

title: When Product Placement Goes Wrong: The Effects of Program Liking and Placement Prominence
finding: Experiment: per authors, prominent placements shift brand attitude negatively among viewers who like the programme a lot, while viewers with lower programme liking shift positively after a prominent placement.
why_for_us: The fans we work hardest to win are the ones punished by heavy-handed product moments; as the series builds a following, make integration subtler, not louder.

title: The Effectiveness of Brand Placements in the Movies: Levels of Placements, Explicit and Implicit Memory, and Brand-Choice Behavior
finding: Experiment with three placement levels (background prop to instrumental part of the story): per authors, placement level influences recognition of and attitudes toward the brand, while even simple background placement affects implicit memory and an implicit choice task.
why_for_us: Use both levels: the assistant as a story instrument in some episodes and as a quiet on-screen presence (open on the office computer) in the others - the background appearances still register implicitly.

title: More than meets the eye: Investigating the hidden impact of brand placements in television magazines
finding: Experiment with an authentic broadcast: per authors, frequently shown placements improve brand evaluation even without recall (mere exposure), but only with high programme involvement and low persuasion knowledge; with high persuasion knowledge and low involvement, frequent placements worsen brand attitudes.
why_for_us: Notaries will have high persuasion knowledge (they know it is vendor content), so repetition only helps if the episodes are genuinely involving; frequency without entertainment backfires.

title: Using Eye Tracking to Understand the Effects of Brand Placement Disclosure Types in Television Programs
finding: Eye-tracking experiment (N=149): per authors, text plus a product-placement logo was the most effective disclosure for advertising recognition (logo alone least); the effect ran through visual attention to the disclosure and the placement, and recognition increased brand memory but led to more negative brand attitudes.
why_for_us: Because our series is openly branded, expect the memory gain and the attitude cost of recognised persuasion; offset the cost with real entertainment/usefulness rather than by hiding the sender.

title: Using Drama to Persuade
finding: 40 TV commercials rated on a dramatization scale and shown to 1,215 people: per authors, arguments are processed evaluatively and dramas empathically, and the evaluative and empathic measures are weighted differently for the two forms.
why_for_us: A drama episode is judged by 'does this feel true' rather than 'is this claim proven' - so verisimilitude of office life matters more than feature claims, and mixing in a lecture switches the viewer back to counter-arguing.

title: Why Narrative Ads Work: An Integrated Process Explanation
finding: Study of a random sample of 25 narrative and 25 non-narrative TV commercials with 484 non-student participants: per authors, four process variables - emotive response, ad hedonic value, ad credibility and perceived goal facilitation - together mediate the positive effect of narrative (vs non-narrative) ads on attitude toward the ad.
why_for_us: Four things to engineer and test per episode: does it move people, is it fun, is it believable, and does the viewer see how the product helps reach a goal of their own.

title: Media engagement and advertising: Transportation, matching, transference and intrusion
finding: Three experiments: per authors, high narrative transportation helps an ad that is not intrusive and thematically matches the narrative, but an ad that interrupts the narrative disrupts transportation and is hurt by it; transportation can also transfer from programme to a non-intrusive ad.
why_for_us: Place the explicit product/CTA card after the story resolves, never in the middle of a tense beat, and keep it thematically continuous with the episode.

title: The Impact of Advertisements and Product Placement (PPL) in Short Dramas on the Consumption Behavior of Middle-Aged and Older Adults
finding: Survey + SEM of middle-aged and older consumers (N not stated in abstract): per authors, plot relevance of ads/PPL in short dramas positively affects brand attitude and purchase intention; brand attitude partially mediates; brand familiarity and short-drama involvement strengthen the effect.
why_for_us: The only record found that tests plot connection inside short dramas themselves, and on a 40+ audience: plot relevance again wins, and works better for a brand the viewer already knows - so pair the series with brand-familiarity touchpoints (email, events). Weak venue, self-report.

title: Managing the content of LinkedIn posts: Influence on B2B customer engagement and sales?
finding: Single-firm time series (VARX on 106 weeks of data from a growing B2B service firm; post types sales/technical/social): per authors, followers and website visits raise sales revenue; sales posts and website visits drive follower growth; social posts, new followers and revenue raise engagement.
why_for_us: On LinkedIn, entertaining 'social' posts (our episodes) buy engagement, but revenue came via followers and site visits - so each episode post needs a route to the site and should be interleaved with plain product posts. One firm only.

title: B2B social media content: engagement on LinkedIn
venue: Journal of Business and Industrial Marketing
finding: Participatory action research on one medium-sized Swedish company's LinkedIn account: per authors, action-oriented messages had a more significant impact on engagement than product-oriented and value-based messages.
why_for_us: Caption episodes with a concrete invitation to do something (try the draft, answer a question) rather than a product description or a values statement. Single case.

title: Business to business digital content marketing: marketers’ perceptions of best practice
venue: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
finding: Qualitative (semi-structured interviews with 15 key informants in USA, UK, France, five sectors): per authors, valuable B2B content is useful, relevant, compelling and timely, needs a 'publishing' mindset and a shift from 'selling' to 'helping', and is seen as a route to trusted-brand status.
why_for_us: Each episode should leave the notary with something useful (a real drafting pitfall, a deadline trap) so the series reads as helping, with the product as the means.

title: Digital content marketing on social media along the B2B customer journey: The effect of timely content delivery on customer engagement
finding: Experimental approach: per authors, exposure to firm content the customer deems relevant at their journey stage raises engagement with the firm and its content, but there is no universally correct sequence of content across stages - preferred content types vary between individuals.
why_for_us: Do not hard-wire one funnel order (awareness episode -> demo -> case story); let email recipients choose their next piece and segment by what they clicked.

title: Fostering brand engagement and value-laden trusted B2B relationships through digital content marketing: The role of brand’s helpfulness
finding: Online survey of a large B2B brand's email list (CB-SEM; N not in abstract): per authors, helpful brand actions (relevant topics, problem-solving orientation, effort to interpret and explain) foster relationship value and brand trust, but only via cognitive-emotional brand engagement.
why_for_us: Helpfulness alone is not enough; it must be emotionally engaging to convert into trust - the argument for wrapping practical notarial tips in a story sent to the email list.

title: Informational vs. emotional B2B firm-generated-content on social media engagement: Computerized visual and textual content analysis
finding: Platform data (5,362 single-image Instagram posts from 10 B2B companies in five industries, automated visual/text analysis): per authors, informational cues drive viewer engagement more than emotional cues, and informational cues work even better in the visual than in the text.
why_for_us: For a B2B audience on Instagram, show the information on screen (the document, the clause, the saved minutes) rather than relying on mood; the thumbnail/first frame should carry a concrete informational cue.

title: The Influence of B to B Social Media Message Features on Brand Engagement: A Fluency Perspective
finding: Twitter data (feeds of the top 50 social B2B brands, 2015): per authors, hashtags and text difficulty correlate with lower likes/retweets, embedded images and video with higher engagement, and B2B tweets get more engagement on evenings and weekends.
why_for_us: Write plain, short captions with few hashtags, always attach the video natively, and test evening/weekend slots - professionals engage with B2B content off-hours.

title: The emotional side of organizational decision-making: examining the influence of messaging in fostering positive outcomes for the brand
finding: Mixed methods (interviews with content developers at a Fortune 100 tech company; web survey of that company's buyer panel): per authors, emotion-themed advertising fosters brand engagement and advocacy, and is especially effective for C-level buyers; greater reliance on facts increases receptivity to emotional advertising.
why_for_us: Supports aiming emotional storytelling at the decision-maker (the notary who owns the office), not only at staff; fact-driven people were more, not less, receptive.

title: Emotional appeals in UK business-to-business financial services advertisements
finding: Content analysis of 834 print ads + 17 interviews with business owners: per authors, emotional appeals are present and noticed, but owners describe a largely utilitarian, need- and benefit-driven decision process; emotional appeals only arouse interest and should be paired with detailed rational information.
why_for_us: Treat the drama as the interest-getter and always attach the rational layer (what it does, price, security, RODO) one click away.

title: What Makes Online Content Viral?
finding: Platform data (all New York Times articles over three months) plus experiments: per authors, positive content is more viral than negative, and high-arousal emotions (awe, anger, anxiety) increase sharing while low-arousal sadness decreases it, controlling for surprise, interest and practical usefulness (each also positively linked to virality) and for prominence.
why_for_us: Aim each episode at an activating feeling (amused recognition, the anxiety of a near-miss deadline then relief) plus practical usefulness; avoid wistful or melancholic endings.

title: What Drives Virality (Sharing) of Online Digital Content? The Critical Role of Information, Emotion, and Brand Prominence
finding: Two field studies of video ads (11 emotions, 60+ ad characteristics) plus an out-of-sample test: per authors, information-focused content reduces sharing except in risky contexts; amusement, excitement, inspiration and warmth increase it; prominent brand placement (early, long, persistent) hurts sharing; emotional ads are shared more on Facebook/Twitter than on LinkedIn, where informational ads do better; sharing peaks at 1.2-1.7 minutes.
why_for_us: Our 60-90 s length sits at the sharing optimum; keep the brand late and brief for Facebook/Instagram cuts, and make a more informational cut for LinkedIn.

title: The Emotions that Drive Viral Video
finding: Two large video data sets (commercial and non-commercial, n=800) with actual daily sharing: per authors, high-arousal emotions are the primary driver of video sharing; valence plays a smaller role.
why_for_us: Intensity beats pleasantness: a mildly nice episode will not be forwarded - push the comic or tense peak higher.

title: Emotions in Online Content Diffusion
finding: WeChat platform data (387,000 news articles, sharing paths of more than six million users; econometric models): per authors, content expressing anxiety, love or surprise spreads farther and forms deeper, broader cascades, whereas anger, sadness and even joy dampen propagation; effects vary with sharer and tie strength.
why_for_us: In private-messenger sharing (how colleagues forward things) surprise and 'constructive uncertainty' travelled, joy alone did not - build the forwardable moment on an unexpected insight about the job.

title: Cracking Jokes and Crafting Selves: Sensemaking and Identity Management Among Human Service Workers
finding: Qualitative (interviews and participant observation among correctional officers, 911 call-takers and firefighters): per authors, workplace humour serves identity needs through differentiation, superiority, role distance and relief, and works as a sensemaking vehicle.
why_for_us: Occupational humour works when it affirms the group's identity against outsiders and absurd job demands; write jokes where the notary and staff are the competent insiders and the laugh falls on the situation, never on the profession.

title: Cooking with humor: In-group humor as social organization
venue: Humor - International Journal of Humor Research
finding: Year-long ethnography of a hotel kitchen (qualitative): per author, chefs' in-group humour is a communicative process that sets the group's boundaries and members' identity and shapes how the group makes sense of and performs its work.
why_for_us: Running gags and insider vocabulary mark who belongs; a recurring catchphrase only notaries fully get can make sharing an act of membership. Indirect evidence (not about media sharing).

title: Disclaimer! This Content Is AI-Generated: How AI-Disclosures Influence Trust in Advertisements and Organizations
finding: Between-subjects experiment (N=304, generative-AI ad with vs without disclosure): per authors, disclosure increased conceptual AI knowledge and attitudinal persuasion knowledge, lowering trust in the ad and the organisation; a positive path also appeared in which disclosure-raised persuasion knowledge increased trust.
why_for_us: Labelling episodes as AI-generated has a trust cost and a smaller transparency benefit; disclose (law and honesty require it) but in a way that signals craft and openness rather than a bare warning label.

title: Is this real or Fake? Examining the effects of disclosure of AI-generated content and source type in instagram-based travel destination advertising on consumer attitudes and behavioral intentions
finding: Two experiments (N=395; N=201) on Instagram ad posts: per authors, disclosure helped recognition of AI origin for a business and for influencers; for human influencers, disclosing AI-generated posts lowered brand credibility, attitude and purchase intention; attitude toward AI moderated the recognition-credibility link.
why_for_us: The penalty falls where viewers expect a real person; fictional characters in an openly fictional series are a safer use of AI than a synthetic 'real notary' testimonial - never present AI characters as real customers.

title: Disclosure in AI-Generated Advertising: How Source Credibility Affects Consumer Purchase Intention
venue: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
finding: Two studies: per authors, disclosing that an ad is AI-generated enhanced perceived ad trustworthiness and attractiveness, improving attitudes and purchase intention; a 'benefit' framing of the disclosure improved ad attitudes while a 'behaviour' framing raised privacy concerns. Sample sizes not in abstract.
why_for_us: Contradicts MD045/MD046: disclosure can help when framed as a benefit - test a line like 'made with AI so we can publish weekly' against a neutral label.

title: Minds Versus Codes: Triangulating Neurophysiological and Qualitative Responses to AI‐Generated Versus Human‐Made Video Advertisements
finding: Laboratory experiment (EEG + eye tracking + participants' reflections; N not in abstract): per authors, AI-generated video ads matched or outperformed human-made ads in evoking emotional responses (surprise, fascination, empathy), and viewers sceptical of AI's emotional authenticity revised their attitude after exposure.
why_for_us: AI video can carry emotion, and exposure reduces scepticism - an argument for letting sceptics simply watch an episode; small lab study, so treat as encouraging rather than settled.

title: Synthetic versus human voices in audiobooks: The human emotional intimacy effect
finding: Experiment comparing stories told by human vs synthetic voice (self-report, physiological response, recognition): per authors, listeners enjoyed human narration more, formed more mental images, were more engaged and attentive, responded more positively and remembered more.
why_for_us: Voice is the weak link of AI storytelling: use the most expressive current engine, keep lines short, and screen every take for flat prosody - the 2021 result reflects older TTS but sets the bar we must clear.

title: The Persuasiveness of Synthetic Speech versus Human Speech
venue: Human Factors The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
finding: Experiment (N=193; high-quality synthetic, low-quality synthetic or human voice delivering a persuasive appeal): per authors, the human voice and speaker were perceived more favourably, but there was no evidence that synthetic speech changed persuasion or perception of the message.
why_for_us: Liking of the voice and persuasion by the message are separable: a synthetic voice may cost warmth without costing the argument. Very old TTS; background only.

title: The Influence of Synthetic Voice on the Evaluation of a Virtual Character
finding: Controlled experiment with a rendered virtual character: per authors, a real human voice was rated more expressive, understandable and likeable than an expressive synthetic voice, yet voice type did not significantly change character-level judgements (appeal, credibility, human-likeness, voice-character match).
why_for_us: Viewers judge the character as a whole; a less-liked voice did not sink the character's credibility - consistent character design may matter more than squeezing the last naturalness out of the voice.

title: A Mismatch in the Human Realism of Face and Voice Produces an Uncanny Valley
finding: Experiment: per authors, a mismatch between the human realism of a character's face and of its voice causes it to be evaluated as eerie.
why_for_us: Match realism levels: a photoreal AI face needs a fully natural voice, or else stylise the visuals so a slightly synthetic voice fits - mismatch, not artificiality itself, is what reads as creepy.

title: Will virtual influencers overcome the uncanny valley? The moderating role of social cues
finding: Two experiments: per authors, highly anthropomorphised virtual influencers elicit more uncanniness, which mediates the effect on consumer intentions; in the presence of social cues the effect of anthropomorphism on uncanniness is attenuated.
why_for_us: Near-human AI characters need social context around them (other characters, interaction, a lived-in office) to defuse eeriness - favour ensemble scenes over a lone talking head.

title: When Less Is More: Content Strategies for Subscription Video on Demand
finding: Field experiment on a streaming platform: per authors, gradual content release boosts engagement and retention more than binge (all-at-once) release. The OpenAlex abstract is one sentence; no effect sizes available.
why_for_us: The strongest causal evidence found for dripping episodes on a schedule rather than dropping all eight at once.

title: The impact of binge watching on memory and perceived comprehension
finding: Controlled experiment (binge vs daily vs weekly viewing schedules; N not in abstract): per authors, binge viewing gives strong memory right after viewing that decays faster than after daily or weekly schedules, and binge viewers reported significantly less enjoyment (authors note caveats).
why_for_us: Spaced release improves what viewers still remember weeks later - which is what a brand needs; a daily or weekly cadence beats a one-day dump for durable recall of the product.

title: Investigating Responses to Narrative Cliffhangers Using Affective Disposition Theory
finding: Two between-subjects experiments with written narratives (N=202; N=273): per authors, cliffhanger endings made audiences want the next instalment more than protagonist-victory endings (both studies) and antagonist-victory endings (Study 2), with no significant difference in enjoyment or suspense.
why_for_us: End episodes on an open question: it raises demand for the next one at no measured cost to enjoyment - then close the loop in the first seconds of the next episode. Tested on text, not video.

title: The Upworthy Research Archive, a time series of 32,487 experiments in U.S. media
finding: Data paper: an archive of 32,487 randomised A/B experiments by Upworthy, each testing variations of a headline-and-image 'package' and recording how many randomly assigned viewers selected each variation. Describes the dataset; no single effect reported in the abstract read.
why_for_us: Evidence that title+thumbnail is a unit worth testing per item, and a public benchmark for how packaging tests are run; adopt the practice of two or three title/thumbnail packages per episode.

title: Optimizing Content with A/B Headline Testing: Changing Newsroom Practices
finding: Interview study in US newsrooms (qualitative): per authors, newsrooms may audience-test as many as a dozen headlines per article with algorithms converging on the best by click-through rate, which changes workflow and headline-writing practice.
why_for_us: Write many titles per episode and let data pick, but with a tiny B2B audience optimise on watch-through or replies rather than click-through alone, since samples will be small.
